analysis.one_liner: Halts new mountaintop removal coal mining permits until federal health studies rule out health risks.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote or even a committee hearing record; it died in committee in the 112th Congress with 27 House Democrats behind it and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have paused all new federal permits for mountaintop removal coal mining — blasting off mountain ridges to reach coal seams in Kentucky, Tennessee, West Virginia, and Virginia — until federal health agencies completed comprehensive studies. If those studies found any health risk to nearby communities, no new permits could be issued at all. Mining companies already operating would have had to continuously monitor and publicly report air, water, noise, and soil pollution, and would have paid a one-time fee to cover the cost of the studies and monitoring.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities surrounding mountaintop removal mining sites in central Appalachia. The bill would have stopped new permits until the government could say whether the mining is making them sick, and given current operations a public, searchable record of the pollution they release. Federal health agencies would have gained funding and a mandate to study a question local residents had raised for years.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any new mountaintop removal permit or expansion under the Clean Water Act or federal mining law until the Secretary of Health and Human Services publishes a determination that the mining presents no health risk to surrounding communities.

Requires the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences to conduct comprehensive studies of health impacts on nearby residents, in response to peer-reviewed research already linking the practice to elevated birth defects, hospitalizations, and mortality.

Requires companies with existing operations to continuously monitor water, air, and noise pollution and frequently monitor soil, submitting results monthly for publication in a public searchable database within seven days.
Finances the studies and monitoring through a one-time fee on companies conducting mountaintop removal projects, rather than general taxpayer funds.

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies conducting mountaintop removal mining. They would face a moratorium on new permits and expansions, a one-time fee covering the federal cost of the studies, and ongoing monitoring and public reporting requirements. Coal-dependent towns and workers in the four states could also bear indirect costs if new projects stopped.

drawbacks.text: The bill's trigger is absolute: permits could only resume after a federal determination that mountaintop removal poses 'no health risk.' Since studies could plausibly find some elevated risk, the moratorium could become a de facto permanent ban rather than a pause pending evidence.

A permit moratorium would stop new mining projects in a region where coal mining is a major employer, imposing real job and local-government revenue costs on coal communities in Kentucky, Tennessee, West Virginia, and Virginia.

The health evidence cited in the bill's findings was largely associational — elevated rates of birth defects and disease persisting after controlling for other variables — and the bill's pre-approval stance meant acting before the studies it orders were completed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the residents of mountaintop removal communities, the bill offered something they otherwise could not get: a federal study of their health complaints and a public record of pollution at nearby sites, with industry paying the bill. The cost falls mainly on mining companies and, indirectly, on coal-dependent towns. The design flaw is the zero-risk standard: rather than a decision rule for how much risk is tolerable, it sets a bar that a finding of any risk would block. That makes the bill closer to an outright ban than a study-then-decide framework, which is the strongest good-faith objection to it — and also why the coal industry and its allies would fight it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, then to two subcommittees, and nothing further ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on June 19, 2012, with 26 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The Speaker referred it to the Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce Committees.
Within a week it was sent to the Water Resources and Environment subcommittee and the Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee.
No committee or subcommittee reported the bill, no hearing or markup appears in the record, and no vote was ever taken in either chamber before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mountaintop removal coal operators came out ahead: permitting continued under existing rules, with no new health studies, no public pollution reporting, and no fees. Residents of nearby communities gained nothing; the federal health studies were never mandated.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill placing a moratorium on mountaintop removal permits until federal health studies were complete.

for.name: 26 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Louise Slaughter, John Yarmuth, Raul Grijalva, Keith Ellison, and Donna Edwards.

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee for a hearing, markup, or vote in the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 26 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral in a chamber whose committees were chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would bar new permits and expansions until a federal determination that the mining poses no health risk, and would impose continuous pollution monitoring, public reporting, and a one-time fee on existing operations. The public health questions the bill targets center on these companies' operations.

industries.industry: Central Appalachian coal-dependent towns and workers
industries.note: A permit moratorium would curb a practice linked in peer-reviewed research to elevated disease and birth defects in surrounding communities, but would also stop new projects in a region where coal mining provides jobs and local tax revenue.
